items.title: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, October 2026
items.description: Zillow: CPI Shelter Forecast, October 2026 Zillow forecasts 2.8% rent inflation, 3.3% OER inflation annually in October, as measured by the Consumer Price Index. Written by Treh Manhertz on October 27, 2026 New shelter inflation numbers from the Bureau of Labor Statistics are scheduled to be released on Friday, November 10, 2026 at 8:30 ET. Key Takeaway CPI housing inflation is expected to stay elevated through the end of the year and into 2027. We currently forecast annual rent inflation to finish 2026 up around 3.1% and OER up near 3.4%. September’s reading on Owners’ Equivalent rates showed growth at the upper end of expectations, but this is unlikely to be the start of a great rise. Shelter disinflation has effectively plateaued in the near-term. New-lease rents have been growing at their fastest pace of 2025-2026, putting a damper on the declines in measured housing inflation. Forecasts for on-market rents have been revised higher for the past few months. Current trends suggest that by year-end, the annual rate of growth will be roughly equal between new-lease rents and CPI rents, keeping a floor under inflation. Multifamily: Zillow’s expectations for on-market rent growth for apartments was revised up: Multifamily rents are expected to rise 2.5% year-over-year in 2026. Methodology These forecasts are based on predictions from a model that makes explicit the relationship between on market rents (measured by the Zillow’s Observed Rent Index) and the shelter components of the Consumer Price Index (CPI). The model incorporates: Expected on-market rent growth (Zillow’s Observed Rent Forecast, ZORF) Assumptions about how landlords adjust rents at lease renewal Renter mobility rates, which determine what share of tenants face a market rent increase. items.title: Select Markets Drive U.S. Office Market Recovery
items.description: Select Markets Drive U.S. Office Market Recovery Oct 29, 2026 U.S. Office Market Outlook Report | Q3 2026 Download Report Experts Marianne Skorupski Director, National Office Research Matthew Gannon Executive Managing Director | Washington D.C. & Head of Agency Leasing | U.S. Jodie Poirier President, Occupier Services & Agency Leasing Market Summary The U.S. office market strengthened in Q3 2026, with the national vacancy rate declining to 17.7%, down 60 basis points from one year ago and the lowest level since Q4 2023. Positive net absorption continued for a ninth consecutive quarter, while demand remained concentrated in high-quality Class A and trophy office buildings across major markets, including New York, San Francisco, Boston, and Seattle. Limited development activity and declining sublease availability are supporting occupancy and rent growth in top-performing assets. Key Findings The U.S. office vacancy rate declined to 17.7% in Q3 2026 , down 20 basis points quarter-over-quarter and 60 basis points year-over-year, marking the lowest level since Q4 2023. Net absorption totaled 9.5 million square feet during Q3 2026, extending a streak of positive absorption to nine consecutive quarters. Total available U.S. office sublease space fell to 150.9 million square feet , down 15.8% year-over-year and marking the 12th consecutive quarter of decline. Earnings Press Release
Invitation Homes Reports Third Quarter 2026 Results
Dallas, TX, October 28, 2026 — Invitation Homes Inc. (NYSE: INVH) (“Invitation Homes,” “we,” “our,” and “us”), the nation’s
premier single-family home leasing and management company, today announced our Third Quarter (“Q3”) 2026 financial and
operating results.


Q3 2026 Highlights
•   Year over year, total revenues increased 6.3% to $731 million, property operating and maintenance costs increased 2.0% to
    $264 million, and net income available to common stockholders increased 15.6% to $158 million, or $0.27 per diluted
    common share.
•   Year over year, Core FFO per share increased 2.4% to $0.48, while AFFO per share increased 0.1% to $0.38.
•   Same Store NOI increased 1.1% year over year on 1.6% Same Store Core Revenues growth and 2.5% Same Store Core
    Operating Expenses growth.
•   Same Store Average Occupancy was 96.4%, a reduction of 10 basis points year over year.
•   Same Store renewal rent growth of 4.3% and Same Store new lease rent growth of (0.2)% resulted in Same Store blended
    rent growth of 3.0%.
•   We sold 658 wholly owned homes, most to families purchasing for their own use, and acquired 216 wholly owned homes,
    for net dispositions of 442 homes and net proceeds of approximately $245 million that we used to fund share repurchases.
•   As previously announced, on July 8, 2026, we closed a public offering of $500 million aggregate principal amount of 4.950%
    senior notes (the “Notes”). The Notes were priced at 99.291% of the principal amount and mature on February 1, 2032. Net
    proceeds were used to prepay a portion of our secured debt obligation maturing in June 2027.


Capital Allocation Update
From December 1, 2025 through October 27, 2026, we bought back nearly $1 billion of our shares. This includes an aggregate
of 36,923,753 shares repurchased to date at an average stock price of $26.78, and represents an implied value per home of
approximately $280,000 against a gross average sales price of approximately $460,000 for homes sold during that same period.


On October 26, 2026, our board of directors authorized an additional $500 million share repurchase program.


Comments from Chief Executive Officer Dallas Tanner
“Our third quarter reflected steady execution across the platform. Same Store NOI grew 1.1% year over year, blended rent growth
was 3.0%, and with the benefit of our share repurchases, Core FFO per share grew 2.4%. Since December 2025, we’ve
repurchased nearly $1 billion of our stock at a substantial valuation discount. We believe that is more than any other residential
REIT. With the new $500 million share repurchase program our board just authorized, we intend to keep funding buybacks with
home sale proceeds whenever our stock trades at a meaningful discount to the value of our homes, guided by market conditions
and a disciplined approach to the balance sheet.”


“Following a solid third quarter, we are raising our full year guidance midpoints for Core FFO per share by $0.01 to $1.96, Same
Store NOI growth guidance to 1.2%, and wholly owned home sales to $950 million, which supports our continued focus on
closing the gap between public and private market values.”

Invitation Homes management that are measures not defined under accounting principles generally accepted in the United States

items.title: Apartment List National Rent Report
items.description: Apartment List National Rent Report By: Chris Salviati and Rob Warnock October 28, 2026 Headline Market Update: November 2026 Year-over-year rent growth in the U.S. flipped positive in October for the first time since mid-2023, though just barely. The national median rent currently stands at $1,384, and is now 0.1% greater than it was at this time last year. The vacancy rate is also gradually tightening, as the market transitions out of the soft conditions that have prevailed in recent years. That said, our newest market indicator tracking the concession rate, continues to show signs of softness. Key Stats National Median Rent: $1,384 per month as of October 2026. Year-Over-Year Rent Growth: Rents are up 0.1% compared to October 2025, marking the first time in over three years that year-over-year rent growth is positive. Month-Over-Month Rent Growth: Rents decreased 0.3% in October 2026 as the rental market enters its off-season; this marks the second consecutive monthly decline. Vacancy Rate: The national multifamily vacancy rate sits at 7% as of October 2026, remaining elevated compared to long-run norms, but continuing to decline after peaking earlier this year. Time on Market: Units are taking an average of 36 days to get leased after being listed, a bit longer than is typical for this time of year. Concessions Rate: 32% of multifamily properties nationally are offering concessions on new leases valued at one month of free rent or greater in October. The concessions rate remains four percentage points higher than at this time last year. Year-over-year rent growth flips positive for first time in over three years For years, the U.S. rental market has been experiencing a prolonged period of sluggishness, as a large wave of multifamily construction had been driving soft pricing and occupancy. However, we’re now at the tail end of that construction boom, and the market has been gradually moving toward more balanced conditions. This month’s data marks a significant milestone in that transition, as year-over-year rent growth flipped positive for the first time in over three years. Following a period of booming rent growth in 2021 and 2022, prices began to cool rapidly, and by June 2023, the national median rent was declining on a year-over-year basis. Full year rent growth was negative for three consecutive years, with prices nationally dipping by -0.8 percent in 2023, by -0.5 percent in 2024, and by -1.2 percent in 2026. Year-over-year rent growth bottomed out at -1.6 percent in April 2026, but over the past six months it has rebounded rapidly as healthy renter demand has filled vacant units and allowed property owners and operators to regain some pricing leverage. Despite the bounceback, rents are still essentially flat compared to one year ago, and are still declining in inflation-adjusted terms. Nonetheless, it’s a significant milestone for the rental market that year-over-year rent growth has now flipped positive. Even as year-year-over rent growth continues to rise, month-over-month rent growth remained negative in October, as the market experiences its typical off-season pricing dip. Fewer renters tend to move in the fall in winter months, and so property owners offer modest discounts to attract demand and fill vacant units at this time of year. But compared to recent years, this year’s fall cooldown has been significantly more subdued. Rents fell by just 0.3 percent in October compared to September; in October of last year, the month-over-month decline was nearly three times as sharp at -0.8 percent. In fact this month’s decline was even slightly more modest than the 2017 to 2019 average (-0.4 percent), a period when the national rental market was in a well-balanced state. In dollar terms, the national median monthly rent now stands at $1,384, up just $1 compared to October 2025. Prices peaked in mid-2022, and have since fallen from that peak by a total of 4 percent, or $58 per month. The national median rent also recently hit a notable milestone – years of modest declines have now offset the rapid price growth that preceded it such that prices are converging back to their long run trend. After oscillating between alternating hot and cool spells throughout the 2020s, the national median rent today is roughly where it would have been if rents had continued to grow at a slow and steady pace of +2.5 percent annually, the average rent growth from 2017 to 2019. This convergence has occurred just as rent growth appears set to stabilize back to something resembling that late-2010s average. Our new concessions rate indicator continues to show some softness This month, in an effort to continue providing actionable, real-time data on the rental market, the Apartment List Economics Team is adding a new dataset to our suite of market indicators: concession rates. Properties that are struggling with occupancy often employ concessions as a strategy for securing new leases. Concessions can take many forms, including discounted rents, cash back offers, gift cards, or free amenities. Such concessions are not factored into our rent estimates, and so tracking them separately provides additional nuance on market conditions. Our published concession rate represents the share of properties offering any discount whose total value is equal to one free month of rent or greater. As of October, 32 percent of all properties are offering concessions valued at one month of free rent or greater. The current concession rate is four percentage points higher than this time last year, when 28 percent of properties were offering such discounts. The concession rate has also ticked up very slightly over the past two months as we enter the off-season. items.title: New Home Sales Declined in September as Builders Focused on Inventory Management
items.description: New Home Sales Declined in September as Builders Focused on Inventory Management Written by Kenny Lee on October 27, 2026 What happened New home sales fell slightly by 0.6% to 676 thousand SAAR in September, essentially holding firm at 680 thousand in August but 5.3% below a year ago. The median price of new homes sold declined 3.9% from a year ago, to $400,400. As homebuilders delay new construction, the number of new homes on the market fell 2.3% year over year to 476 thousand homes in September — marking the 11th consecutive month of annual decline. Inventory adjustment has been a counterbalance to cooler inventory. At the latest sales pace, it would take about 8.4 months to clear the inventory, up slightly from 8.2 months a year ago. Smaller and more affordable units constituted a larger share of total sales, with 70% of homes selling below $500,000 in September. As elevated mortgage rates keep buyers on the sidelines, the share will likely continue to rise. By comparison, 66% of new homes sold were below this price point in September last year. Inventory management would remain the number one priority for builders For builders, the ongoing shift toward smaller homes was prudent and necessary. While mortgage rates soared above 7% in September, homebuilders have been navigating elevated rates, in addition to their wild swings, for a while. Builders will remain focused on inventory management, especially as competition from the resale market increases. Zillow’s September report shows resale inventory rose 2.5% year over year, marking the 34th consecutive month of annual gains. In addition, 27.4% of sellers reduced asking prices as they adapt to shifting buyer demand. Building smaller homes is a win-win for both buyers and builders. For buyers, a lower entry point helps them navigate the challenging affordability landscape. For builders, they can keep their inventory moving even as buyers see more options in the resale market. items.title: S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index Reports Annual Gain in August 2026 - Oct 27, 2026
items.description: Press Releases Media Contacts Social Media Directory Press Kit Press Releases S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index Reports Annual Gain in August 2026 The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index posted a 2.1% annual gain for August 2026, up from a 1.9% rise in the previous month. U.S. home values fell in real terms for the 15th consecutive month, as August's 3.4% inflation ran roughly 1.3 percentage points above the 2.1% home price gain. A nearly 9 percentage point gap separated August's strongest market (Chicago +6.7% YoY) and its weakest (Seattle -2.0% YoY), underscoring the strong regional divergence in home price trends. NEW YORK , Oct. 27, 2026 / PRNewswire / -- S&P Dow Jones Indices (S&P DJI) today released the August 2026 results for the S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Indices. More than 27 years of history are available for the data series and can be accessed in full by going to www.spglobal.com/spdji/en/index-family/indicators/sp-Cotality-case-shiller . Cotality continues to have transaction delays from the recording office in Wayne County, the most populous county in the Detroit metro area. These delays impacted the August transaction data and, therefore, no valid August 2026 update of the Detroit S&P Cotality Case-Shiller Index will be provided for the October 27, 2026, release date. There was, however, enough data to calculate a valid July 2026 update, which is provided in Tables 2 and 3. S&P DJI will continue to provide updates to the Detroit index values for the month(s) with missing sale transactions data. ANALYSIS "U.S. home prices declined in real terms for the 15th consecutive month in August 2026, though the gap narrowed as nominal home price growth strengthened," said Rebecca Kaufman, Associate Director of Commodities at S&P Dow Jones Indices. "The S&P CoreLogic Case-Shiller National Home Price Index rose 2.1% year-over-year in August, up from 1.9% in July, while consumer prices increased 3.4% (the same year over year gain as in July 2026). "Chicago led all metros for the sixth consecutive month, posting a 6.7% annual gain, followed by New York (6.2%) and Cleveland (4.3%). On the West coast, Seattle recorded the largest annual decline for the third consecutive month at 2.0%, followed by Las Vegas (-1.3%) and Denver (-0.8%). "Seasonality continued to weigh on headline monthly results. On a non-seasonally adjusted basis, the U.S. National and 10-City Composite Indices fell 0.2% and 0.4%, respectively, while their seasonally adjusted counterparts rose 0.3% and 0.4%. The divergence suggests that the typical post-summer slowdown is obscuring some underlying strength in home prices. "Affordability, however, remains challenging. With inflation at 3.4%, Brent crude near $100 per barrel and mortgage rates in the mid-to-high 6% range, households continue to face elevated costs alongside persistently high home prices." YEAR-OVER-YEAR The S&P Cotality Case-Shiller U.S. National Home Price NSA Index, covering all nine U.S. census divisions, reported a 2.1% annual gain for August. The 10-City Composite saw an annual increase of 3.6%, up from a 3.4% increase in the previous month. The 20-City Composite posted a year-over-year increase of 2.7%, up from a 2.5% rise in the previous month. Chicago reported the highest annual gain among the 20 cities with a 6.7% increase in August, followed by New York and Cleveland with annual increases of 6.2% and 4.3%, respectively. Seattle posted the lowest return in August, falling 2.0%. MONTH-OVER-MONTH The pre-seasonally adjusted U.S. National Index posted a monthly decrease of 0.2%; while both the 10-City Composite and 20-City Composite Indices recorded a monthly decline of 0.4%. After seasonal adjustment, the U.S. National, 10-City, and 20-City Composite Indices posted 0.3%, 0.4%, and 0.3% gains, respectively. items.title: FOMC Leaves Rate Unchanged
items.description: Economic Coverage FOMC Leaves Rate Unchanged By Danielle Hale Oct 28, 2026 The Federal Reserve’s Open Market Committee (FOMC), the rate-setting body that meets roughly eight times per year, left the Federal Funds rate unchanged at its October meeting in a target range of 3.75 to 4.0 percent. This hold follows a 25 basis point hike in September, and was supported by 10 of the 12 voting members. Two voters, Lisa Cook and Beth Hammack, dissented, because they preferred to raise the rate by a quarter percentage point instead of holding. Even though the Fed left its policy rate unchanged in October, the market is anticipating another 2 to 3 hikes over the next 6 to 8 months which would mean a high-end rate range of 4.5 to 4.75 percent. This is slightly above the high-end of Fed funds rate projections made in September, and would position the Fed funds rate roughly halfway between its December 2025 to September 2026 low of 3.5 to 3.75 percent and its 5.25 to 5.5 percent prior peak. While the market and the Fed both seem to agree that some monetary policy restriction is warranted, most investors currently expect more restriction than the Fed has projected. Why further rate hikes are expected Since the September FOMC meeting, when the Fed pushed its rate 25 basis points higher, companies slowed hiring and summer job gains were revised down by 60,000 jobs . The unemployment rate remains relatively stable at 4.2 percent and layoffs are low, but the labor market is less dynamic than is ideal. Meanwhile, inflation surprised to the upside, with the CPI rising 0.6% in September, bringing the annual headline inflation rate to 3.7% as the cost of gas and energy rose sharply. Energy was not the only driver, however, and core CPI, which strips out the cost of food and energy, rose 2.6% in September. Taken together, these indicators suggest that the Fed is likely to continue its focus on inflation, which will likely warrant additional rate hikes. What this means for housing, and homebuyers and sellers Investors have made a round-trip in risk pricing since just before the September Fed meeting. The 10-year yield rose from just under 5 percent to more than 5.3 percent before dipping just under 5 percent in recent days, while mortgage rates climbed from just below 7 percent to more than 7.4 percent. Mortgage rates have not dropped back to their mid-September level, and the housing market is feeling the effects. Pending home sales in September dropped to their lowest level on record according to the National Association of Realtors as buyers and sellers have largely disengaged with the housing market for now. In August and September, existing-home sales dropped below a 4 million sales pace, and are likely to remain low through the rest of the year. Home shoppers shopping in this environment can still set themselves up for a better mortgage rate by boosting their credit, making a higher down payment, and, most importantly, shopping around for a mortgage. Those hoping to make a home purchase in the months ahead should plan for further mortgage rate volatility and rate-proof their home shopping budget by testing out a range of possible mortgage rates so they’ll be prepared to react.

Washington, D.C. – U.S. house prices rose nationwide in August, up 0.3 percent from the previous
month, according to the U.S. Federal Housing (FHFA) seasonally adjusted monthly House Price
Index (FHFA HPI®). House prices rose 2.4 percent from August 2025 to August 2026. The
previously reported 0.3 percent price increase in July was revised down to 0.2 percent.

percent in the New England division to +2.1 percent in the East South Central division. The 12-
month changes ranged from +0.5 percent in the Mountain division to +4.4 percent in the East North
Central division.

The FHFA HPI is a comprehensive collection of publicly available house price indexes that tracks
changes in single-family home values across the United States. The data extend back to the mid-1970s
and cover all 50 states and more than 400 American cities. Drawing on information from over 100
million home sales and refinance transactions, the FHFA HPI provides detailed insights into house price
trends at the national, census division, state, metropolitan area, county, ZIP code, and census tract
levels. FHFA employs a transparent, weighted repeat-sales methodology to measure changes in home
prices using historical housing transaction data.

FHFA releases HPI data and reports quarterly and monthly. The flagship FHFA HPI uses seasonally
adjusted, purchase-only data from Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac. Additional indexes use other data,
including refinances, mortgages insured by the Federal Housing Administration, and real property
records. All the indexes (including their historic values) and information about future HPI release dates
are available on FHFA’s website: https://www.fhfa.gov/HPI.

The next HPI report will be released on November 24, 2026, and will include monthly data through
September 2026 and quarterly data through the third quarter of 2026.

items.title: Weather rewrites home value
items.description: Weather is one of the oldest small talk topics there is, but in hurricane-prone Dare County, North Carolina, it stopped being small talk in 2023. That year, 13% of property insurance policies weren’t renewed, and home values fell about 10%. By 2025, price growth had turned negative. Homeowners did nothing wrong. The weather changed. ‍ For decades, historical knowledge priced environmental risk as floods came on a somewhat predictable schedule, and hurricanes followed predictable seasonal patterns. Insurers wrote policies accordingly. But Cotality's latest data analysis in the United States and Australia shows the arrangement has broken, and that relationship will only become shakier heading into 2040. Historical patterns no longer offer a reliable baseline for what's to come. The weather template is changing — it’s affecting the price of homeowner security, and home values are starting to reflect the difference. ‍ Comparing home price and insurance non-renewals: Dare County, North Carolina Data source: Cotality, 2026 Priced out of safety Miami and Naples in Florida sit among the top three U.S. cities with the most homes exposed to three natural perils simultaneously over the next 30 years. A year ago, both were migration magnets, with median prices outpacing the national average. Now, the tide has turned. Miami's market flatlined in February 2026. Naples saw price growth fall 8.3%, according to Cotality’s Home Price Index. ‍ The impact of natural disasters on real estate Data source: Cotality, 2026 California is home to a similar scenario. The state has some of the highest home prices in the U.S., which limits the buyer pool. Those who do buy a home generally take out a mortgage. That mortgage requires insurance — but getting coverage is no longer a guarantee. Wildfire risk caused many major insurers to stop writing new policies in the state where losses are mounting — Cotality research found that annual wildfire losses are projected to reach $54 million in Nevada County alone over the next 15 years. In areas like Lake County, California, the costs of environmental risk are giving carriers pause, and have pushed the insurance non-renewal rates to 7.6% in 2023. Those who can afford to still buy a home often ask for a risk discount. Environmental risk in homebuying kicks off a downward pricing trend that can depress the market over time. Already, the state has seen negative price growth in 2026. Dive deeper Comprehensive chronic climate risk assessments Between 2026 and 2040, Cotality’s Climate Risk Analytics identified current “safe” markets that will become uninsurable housing markets. Current climate risk averages ‍ Climate risk averages in 2040 Data source: Cotality, 2026 Australia is seeing a similar trend. The three towns flooded in 2022 — Lismore, Mullumbimby, Ballina — sit 5% below their pre-flood values, and buyers haven't returned. Yet, just to the north, coastal South-East Queensland, also flooded, rebounded within months and now sits 31% above pre-flood prices. Lifestyle-driven demand in that region appears to be holding the price up where it can. Where it can't, the weather-driven discount sticks. Climate risk assessment of Australian communities Data source: Cotality, 2026 ‍ "The combination of extensive damage and persistent risk of disruption in these areas of northern New South Wales isn't compensated for by the lifestyle demand seen in coastal suburbs of Queensland," said Richard Griffiths, Cotality's Head of Sustainability Solutions. Don't discount disaster: Environmental risk in homebuying Hurricanes and wildfires in California and Florida tend to get the media attention, but trouble is also present up in the middle of the country, where hail, tornadoes and storms are running up the bill one premium hike at a time. In Winkler, Texas, nearly one in four homeowners had insurance policies dropped. In Kiowa County, Oklahoma, Cotality projects $1.4 million in additional annual storm losses across just 8,800 homes by 2040. The mathematics have tipped to the point that insurance premium and deductible increases in Kiowa County now outpace yearly equity gains. Owners are paying more to protect a home that's earning less. Such rising costs are particularly landing on Gen Z . In Nebraska and Oklahoma, 9% of mortgage applicants are under 25, drawn by lower home prices, but not always seeing the full picture when insurance is factored in. A lower mortgage today can mean a larger insurance bill tomorrow, or a buyer five years out who won't pay what the current owner did. "This is a national challenge in Australia," said Griffiths. "As climate events become more frequent, the gap in how Australian communities experience and recover from disaster will only widen, further exacerbating inequality between more desirable coastal communities and rural areas." items.title: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum
items.description: Gateway Markets Regain Development Momentum by Chuck Ehmann Posted October 29, 2026 in Multifamily Construction Permits Whether you call them “gateway” markets or the “sexy six,” the primary coastal hubs that traditionally attract the majority of domestic and international capital are well represented among the top markets for annual multifamily permitting in September’s data release from the U.S. Census Bureau, and in most cases are dramatically increasing their permitting activity. New York continues to lead the nation for multifamily permitting with 37,691 units permitted in the year-ending September, an increase of more than 13,000 units from last year or a jump of 52.7%. Los Angeles again ranked #2 with about 18,000 units permitted, almost doubling their annual total from one year ago. Washington, DC remained among the top permitting markets at #5 in September, increasing their annual permitting by 47.4% or about 3,900 units, while Seattle slipped to #11 this month but still increased their multifamily permitting total by 36.7% or roughly 2,400 units. Rounding out the “sexy six,” Boston ranked #16 among Realpage’s top 150 markets with a 44.7% annual increase (+2,303 units) to 7,460 units, while the Bay Area markets of San Jose, Oakland and San Francisco ranked well down the list individually but would have ranked #7 with a combined total of 11,543 units permitted, up 46.8% from last year (+5,407 units). Conversely, among the secondary high-growth markets, development activity has stalled or fallen back as top 10 markets Phoenix and Atlanta permitted close to the same amount as last year, while Dallas, Houston, Austin and Miami decreased their permitted unit counts by a combined 11,004 units. Only Raleigh/Durham saw a significant increase in multifamily permitting (+3,153 units) among the non-gateway top 10 markets. Despite declining permitting in four of September’s top 10 markets, their combined total of 148,456 units was up 14.5% from last September for an increase of 18,765 units. Compared to August, the top 10 markets’ annual permitting total was little changed (-0.7%). In addition to the expanding top 10 and the gateway markets mentioned, other markets with significant increases in annual units permitted in September were Kansas City (+2,187 units), West Palm Beach (+1,932 units), College Station-Bryan, TX (+1,762 units), Tacoma (+1,712 units) and Fort Worth (+1,672 units). Orlando (-4,572 units) led for annual permitting decreases, followed by Dallas and Houston. Significant decreases occurred in Columbus, OH (-2,911 units), Riverside-San Bernardino (-2,162 units), San Diego (-2,100 units) and Lakeland-Winter Haven, FL (-1,995 units). Permitting by Place Below the metro level, eight of August’s top 10 permit-issuing places returned to this month’s list with the first five remaining in order. The list of top individual permitting places (cities, towns, boroughs, and unincorporated counties) generally includes the principal city of some of the most active metro areas. The city of Los Angeles again led the nation for multifamily permitting at the local level with New York’s three most active boroughs returning among the top five. The city of Phoenix also placed in the top five while the city of Fort Worth jumped to #6 in September from #10 last month. The cities of Austin and Atlanta each slipped one spot as the cities of Columbus and Houston fell out of the top 10 entirely. The cities of Miami and Denver joined the top 10 list this month, permitting about 5,500 units apiece. Among the top 10 metros for multifamily permitting, Dallas, Houston, Washington, DC and Raleigh/Durham were not represented on the top 10 list of permitting places, although the core cities of Dallas, Houston, Raleigh and Durham were among the top 20 places. Washington, DC’s multifamily permitting was spread diversely around that metro’s area. items.title: PCE Inflation Accelerated in September
items.description: PCE Inflation Accelerated in September October 29, 2026 Fan-Yu Kuo No Comments The Federal Reserve's preferred inflation gauge accelerated in September after holding at 3.0% for three consecutive months, complicating the Fed's path to its 2% target. Consumer spending continued to be pushed up by elevated energy prices rather than income growth, driving the personal saving rate to the lowest level in nearly four years. The headline Personal Consumption Expenditure (PCE) Price Index increased 3.6% in September from a year ago, the fastest pace since May, according to the Bureau of Economic Analysis . The “core” PCE price index, which excludes food and energy, rose 3.1% over the past twelve months, following a 3.0% increase last month. Core PCE has remained at or above 3.0% since the start of the Iran conflict, suggesting inflation pressure persists even excluding volatile energy prices. Consumer spending rose 0.5% in September, while real spending, adjusted to remove inflation, remained unchanged. Meanwhile, personal income rose 0.2% in September. This growth was led by increases in compensation and government social benefits. Real disposable income—income adjusted for taxes and inflation—fell 0.3%. On a year-over-year basis, personal income was 4.1% higher, and real (inflation-adjusted) disposable income was up 1.0%. With spending growth outpacing income growth, the personal saving rate fell to 3.8% in September, the lowest level since November 2022. items.description: New Trump housing order targets mortgage and title insurers A White House plan to pull private mortgage insurance off loans sooner, and to let refinancing borrowers skip the lender's title policy, affects two insurance lines that say they already help keep costs down PROPERTY By Stephen Owens Oct 25, 2026 Share Mortgage insurers and title underwriters are the latest targets of the White House's pre-election push on housing costs. President Donald Trump on Oct. 22 signed an executive order, Decreasing Housing Costs for the American People , that leans on the Federal Housing Finance Agency to squeeze costs out of the mortgage process. Two of its four main provisions deal with insurance: a pilot to cancel mortgage insurance premiums ahead of schedule, and a permanent version of FHFA's experiment letting some refinances skip the traditional lender's title policy, according to the White House fact sheet . The rest of the order sets up a federal task force on factory-built housing and tells the Agriculture and Veterans Affairs departments to cut rates on their direct home loans. FHFA Director Bill Pulte called it "the greatest Housing Executive Order in History" on X. The fact sheet, however, sets no equity thresholds, no start dates and no estimate of how many loans would qualify, so mortgage insurers, title underwriters and agents can't yet tell how much business is at stake. Read next: Why home insurance prices are quietly becoming a 2026 midterm flashpoint Mortgage insurers say cancellation rules already exist The mortgage insurance piece would have Fannie Mae and Freddie Mac use automated valuation models to recheck home values on loans they own from time to time, then drop the coverage once a borrower appears to have built enough equity, according to Mortgage Professional America's breakdown of the order . Servicers would have to tell borrowers when cancellation might be possible. The pilot covers only loans originated after it launches. Borrowers already paying premiums would not benefit directly. Mortgage insurers point out that borrowers already have cancellation rights. Under the federal Homeowners Protection Act, borrower-paid coverage on a conventional loan must end automatically once the balance hits 78% of the home's original value, and borrowers can ask to cancel at 80%, with some able to qualify on the strength of home price gains if conditions are met, according to U.S. Mortgage Insurers (USMI) , the trade group whose members include Enact, Essent, MGIC, National MI and Radian. USMI President Seth Appleton welcomed the focus on costs and said the industry was already lowering them. "Private MI is designed to be temporary, and the system already works much the way the order envisions, because when MI is cancelled, a borrower's monthly payment goes down," he said in the group's statement. USMI's statement describes the order as telling FHFA to consider a pilot, not to launch one. The group says premium rates have fallen 25% since 2017, that more than 800,000 buyers used private coverage in 2025, two-thirds of them first-timers, and that its members insure more than $1.6 trillion in mortgages. Insurers have paid over $62 billion in claims since 2008 that would otherwise have hit the government-sponsored enterprises, lenders and investors, USMI said. The pilot could also affect pricing. Mortgage insurance is priced on how long an insurer expects to keep collecting premiums. Some industry voices warned that a program clipping off late-life, low-risk loans could push insurers to build that lost income into pricing on new business, MPA reported . The order comes during a strong year for mortgage insurers. New insurance written across the six active private insurers (Arch, Enact, Essent, MGIC, NMI and Radian) hit a multi-year high in the second quarter of 2026, with strong credit performance, according to Milliman's quarterly market update . Read next : Old Republic prevails as Massachusetts court rejects title coverage expansion Title waiver pilot would become permanent For title underwriters, the order expands a program their trade group has opposed since 2024. The title acceptance pilot dates to March 2024, when the Biden-era FHFA approved waiving the lender's title policy, or an attorney opinion letter, on certain low-risk refinances where there is confidence the property is free of prior liens, according to a statement from then-Director Sandra Thompson . Fannie Mae launched it in November 2024 with Doma Title Insurance and added Westcor Land Title Insurance Co. in July 2025. Pulte said in June that Fannie would grow it. The order would make the program permanent and broaden it. The order directs FHFA to lift the current 80% loan-to-value cap on eligibility, bring in more title-assessment providers and scrap the geographic limits, according to MPA's reading of the text. It also calls for waiving appraisals and income re-verification on limited cash-out refinances that cut a borrower's monthly payment. The American Land Title Association responded the same day, warning that any cost-cutting push must keep protections for homeowners and their property rights in place rather than shift risk to consumers and taxpayers. In 2024, ALTA called the original pilot a political gesture that offered a false promise of savings. Analysts expect a limited effect for now. Analysts at Keefe, Bruyette & Woods wrote in an Oct. 21 note that refinances account for only about 7% of title premiums, so the earnings hit should be modest while the program stays refi-only. They said the risk would be greater if the waiver ever reached purchase loans, where there is no scalable substitute for a title policy. Refinance volume is low with 30-year rates above 7%, but a rate drop would quickly enlarge the pool of loans eligible for a waiver, and the order would also remove the program's geographic limits. The year-to-date median sale price reached $225,900 per unit.Las Vegas multifamily market overviewLas Vegas multifamily fundamentals remain under pressure despite improved absorption and a slowdown in new deliveries in 2026. Net absorption has exceeded deliveries by roughly 650 units year to date, after trailing them by nearly 1,700 units in 2025. Absorption has already surpassed the full-year 2025 total, supported by continued job growth, while completions have slowed as fewer projects remain under construction. The recovery has been concentrated in the suburbs, where Summerlin/Spring Valley, Henderson and Enterprise/South Paradise captured more than two-thirds of that demand with less than half of the metro’s inventory. Rent growth has been slower to rebound. Asking rents remain below year-ago levels, with the steepest declines in older urban core submarkets, where vacancy is above 10%. By contrast, rents in suburban submarkets remain close to year-ago levels.Investment activity in 2026 has become concentrated in two of the suburban submarkets that are leading the leasing recovery. Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson accounted for roughly three-quarters of metro sales volume through the third quarter, up from 43% in 2025. Third-quarter activity followed the same pattern, with three of the five trades located in those two submarkets. Pricing has remained stable in Summerlin/Spring Valley and Henderson, with median sale prices near $250,000 per unit in both submarkets, above levels elsewhere in the metro, where recent trades have skewed toward smaller, older properties. Six active projects in Spring Valley total more than 2,000 units.Multifamily permitting activity is regaining momentum. items.title: Rocket posts $709M profit in Q3 despite tougher mortgage market
items.description: Rocket Companies on Thursday reported a third-quarter profit of $709 million, reversing a loss from a year ago as the Detroit-based mortgage lender expanded revenue and gained market share in purchase and refinance lending. The company reported net income of $709 million for the three months ended Sept. 30, compared with a net loss of $124 million a year earlier and a second-quarter 2026 net income of $229 million. Net total revenue nearly doubled year over year to $3.28 billion, up from $1.7 billion, while adjusted revenue rose to $2.57 billion, up from $1.87 billion. Adjusted net income fell to $419 million from $441 million in Q2 2026, and adjusted EBITDA declined to $748 million from Q2's $766 million. Mortgage production also slowed, with closed origination volume falling to $43.6 billion, down from $49.1 billion. The sequential decline in adjusted earnings came as mortgage production slowed from the second quarter, even as the company reported a slightly higher gain-on-sale margin. Rocket chief financial officer Brian Brown anticipated the slowdown during the company’s Q2 2026 earnings call, saying he expected Q3 to be “smaller than the second,” a contraction not seen in the industry since 2022. He cited rates above 6.8% and rising inflation expectations as key challenges. “Rocket gained market share in both purchase and refinance, quarter over quarter and year over year, and delivered our highest profitability margin in nearly five years, even as mortgage rates climbed to a three-year high,” CEO Varun Krishna said in a statement. “We didn’t spend the last three years waiting for rates to fall. We acquired distribution, connected real estate and mortgage , and invested heavily in technology. We changed the economics of our business. Rates went up. We took share. Profits grew. That’s not a coincidence.” During the company's earnings call on Thursday afternoon, Krishna addressed the broader market. "Here's the truth about tough markets: They don't lie," he said. "They strip everything down to what's real. Who has the capital to keep investing? Whose model works in any cycle? Who can win their clients back? And who can move fast when it counts? This quarter did all of this." Brown said during the call that the company estimates its purchase market share approached 6.5% in Q3 2026, up from 6.2% in Q2 2026. Its refinance share reached 15.5%, compared with 14.3% from April through June. Mortgage production and servicing Rocket closed $43.6 billion in mortgage originations in the third quarter, down from $49.1 billion in Q2. Net rate-lock volume fell to $40.4 billion from $47 billion over the same period. The company’s total gain-on-sale margin edged up to 2.54% from 2.48% in Q2. Excluding correspondent lending , Rocket closed $33.5 billion in mortgage volume during the third quarter. Direct-to-consumer lending accounted for $24.6 billion, while wholesale channel Rocket Pro generated $9 billion. The correspondent channel contributed $10.1 billion in closed volume. Rocket’s mortgage servicing portfolio remained steady at about $2 trillion in unpaid principal balance across 9.1 million loans. The company sold mortgage servicing rights tied to $23 billion in unpaid principal balance during Q3, generating $379 million in proceeds. That was down from $53 billion in MSR sales and $795 million in proceeds in Q2. Rocket retained subservicing and recapture services on nearly 70% of the servicing rights sold in the third quarter, compared with nearly 80% in Q2. Total liquidity rose to $11.4 billion at the end of Q3, up from $11.2 billion at the end of the prior quarter. The figure includes $2.7 billion in cash, $2.5 billion in undrawn credit lines and $6.2 billion in available servicing-rights and advance lines. Rocket said its combined servicing portfolio following the Mr. Cooper integration continued to support borrower recapture, with the company reaching its highest recapture levels to date. During Q3, Rocket continued to expand its use of artificial intelligence and its partnerships with real estate companies. The company said it pulled credit on nearly 20% of its direct-to-consumer loan volume before borrowers spoke with a loan officer, compared with none a year earlier. Digital mortgage applications accounted for more than 40% of retail refinance applications, and digital leads converted at four times the rate of nondigital leads. AI voice technology handled 65% of inbound servicing calls, resolving more than half without human assistance. Rocket also reported growth in its real estate partnerships. Redfin visitors who clicked to begin a mortgage transaction increased 50% year over year, while Redfin’s contribution to Rocket’s refinance leads more than doubled in Q3. Listings tied to its Compass partnership reached nearly 40,000, up from about 25,000 in Q2. In September, Rocket Mortgage adopted VantageScore 4.0 as its preferred credit scoring model for eligible loans. The company said its testing indicated qualifying borrowers could save an average of $1,600 in closing costs. Rocket Pro launched Orbit in October , offering eligible purchase borrowers same-day conditional approval and a 12-business-day timeline to clear-to-close. The company also extended a Compass pricing credit through the end of 2026. The partnership had generated more than $3 billion in rate locks since February. Supply Miami-Dade County’s retail construction pipeline remained steady in the third quarter of 2026, with 1.3 million square feet (msf) underway. Construction commenced on nearly 63,000 square feet (sf) of new retail space during the quarter. Meanwhile, deliveries totaled 78,000 sf, bringing year-to-date (YTD) deliveries to 158,000 sf. This represented a 64.6% year-over-year (YOY) decrease from the 447,000 sf delivered during the same period in 2025. Vacancy increased 10 basis points (bps) quarter-over-quarter (QOQ) to 3.1% and rose by the same amount YOY. Despite the slight increase, Miami-Dade County’s retail market continued to demonstrate tight conditions, with vacancy remaining the lowest among Florida markets, below Fort Lauderdale at 4.2%, Orlando at 3.9% and Tampa at 3.8%. Demand Retail leasing activity across Miami-Dade County totaled more than 441,000 sf in the third quarter of 2026, bringing YTD deal volume to 1.7 msf, down 18.0% YOY. The market recorded negative 81,000 sf of net absorption during the quarter, bringing the YTD total to negative 129,000 sf. Although occupancy losses have persisted in six of the past seven quarters, quarterly performance improved considerably from negative 230,000 sf in the third quarter of 2025. At the submarket level, Kendall and Miami Airport led occupancy gains, recording 97,000 sf and nearly 51,000 sf of positive absorption, respectively. These gains were offset by losses in Coral Gables (negative 41,000 sf) and Northeast Dade (negative 35,000 sf). By property type, malls posted the strongest performance, with occupancy gains of just under 12,000 sf, while general retail recorded the largest decline at negative 62,000 sf. Overall, leasing activity and occupancy trends remained mixed across the county, with gains in select submarkets and property types offset by continued weakness elsewhere. Looking ahead, the construction pipeline may provide additional opportunities for retailers as new space enters the market, although future occupancy gains will depend on demand keeping pace with new supply. Pricing Miami-Dade County’s average retail asking rent reached $50.27 per square foot (psf) in the third quarter of 2026, representing a 1.8% increase YOY. Among the county’s retail submarkets, Miami Beach commanded the highest average asking rent at $97.85 psf, while Miami recorded the lowest at $31.92 psf. Compared YOY, average asking rents increased in 16 submarkets and declined in three. Outlying Miami-Dade County recorded the largest YOY increase, with rents rising 4.1% from $40.97 psf to $42.65 psf. In contrast, Brickell asking rents declined 2.4% YOY to $84.96 psf. Retail Sales Miami-Dade County recorded $619.9 million in retail investment sales during the third quarter of 2026, representing almost 810,000 sf sold. This brought YTD transaction volume to $1.2 billion across 2.0 msf. YTD transaction volume declined 25.5% YOY and was 6.6% below the five-year average. Miami Airport led all submarkets with $265.8 million in sales. Notable transactions included the $72.0 million sale of Airpark Plaza, located at 5715 NW Seventh Street in the Miami Airport submarket. By property type, strip malls recorded the highest average sale price at $815 psf during the quarter. Pricing remained elevated, with Miami averaging $450 psf, well above the U.S. average of $246 psf, underscoring the market’s continued premium positioning. Miami-Dade County’s retail capitalization rates ranged from 4.9% to 7.2%, averaging 5.8%. This was below the national average of 7.4%, indicating that local retail properties continued to trade at lower yields than the national average. Download Q3 2026 Report For the data behind the commentary, download the full Q3 2026 U.S. Life Sciences Report . The life sciences sector is showing early signs of recovery. Overall vacancy declined in Q3 after four years of steady increases, suggesting a potential market inflection point. Improving fundamentals are laying the foundation for more sustained long-term growth. Q3 2026 Life Sciences Key Trends Absorption turned positive in Q3, totaling nearly 500,000 square feet (sf). Leasing activity also accelerated, increasing 11% quarter-over-quarter (QOQ). Despite stronger demand this quarter, total net absorption remained negative for the year. Asking rents continue to soften, falling 5.6% year-over-year (YOY) to $62.85 per square foot (psf). Some markets, including Los Angeles-Orange County and Philadelphia, saw asking rents grow on a YOY basis. However, rents are expected to continue to soften in the near term until demand strengthens further. The overall vacancy rate dropped 20 basis points (bps) QOQ to 23.9% , marking the first quarterly decline in four years and indicating that vacancy has likely peaked. While there may be some short-term volatility, we expect the vacancy rate to trend lower over the next year. The construction pipeline continues shrink with close to 5.2 million square feet (msf) currently under construction, down 40% from a year ago. The pipeline is overwhelmingly focused on build-to-suit (BTS) projects, which account for 73% of the pipeline. R&D property sales totaled $3 billion in Q3, up 50% YOY , while pricing increased 13% YOY. Deal activity was driven largely by buyers making opportunistic purchases, though interest rate uncertainty may temper activity in the near term. Quarterly venture capital funding declined to $7.9 billion in Q3. However, year-to-date (YTD) funding is up 6% YOY. Average deal size fell 18% YOY to $17 million, indicating that capital may be flowing to early-stage companies. The IPO market remains active, with $7.3 billion in deal volume YTD, nearly four times higher than the same period last year. items.title: Abundance of Single-Family Homes in Houston May Dilute Multifamily Demand
items.description: Abundance of Single-Family Homes in Houston May Dilute Multifamily Demand by Carl Whitaker Posted October 13, 2026 in Insights Houston might be the ficklest market in the country and has been a source of disappointment for owner/operators for what feels like forever now. The metro just can't seem to sustain stretches of consistently robust demand, but that's yet to be a consistent deterrent of new construction activity which thereby compounds local frustration. Houston's rents didn't grow at all in 3rd quarter 2026, and because of that stagnation, rent cuts today are now similar to their COVID-era low point (about 2% rent cuts year-over-year). Class A rent growth just returned this quarter, with prices climbing 1% year-over-year, the first annual increase the segment has seen in four quarters. Granted, Class B rents (down 1.9%) and Class C (down 5.4%) do highlight a story of deeper challenges elsewhere. Houston might be the biggest miss I've had in the past two years. One theory I tend to buy into in Houston is that single family demand poaches demand away from multifamily at a higher-than-usual pace. In fact, multifamily permits make up just 25% of total Houston MSA permitting on average. Only Cleveland, Memphis, Greensboro, Sacramento, Inland Empire, Las Vegas and Indianapolis see a higher skew toward single family. So essentially, Houston demand gets diluted by lots of housing supply (in turn, informing part of this metro's relative affordability). And here in the past year or two, demand has been even more ephemeral with immigration reform and energy sector ups-and-downs.
